claim: 14 EC clusters were identified using the Louvain method for unsupervised community detection.

evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1g, h.

evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3b, d.

source: Notably, triple-positive cells (Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+) were more frequently observed in the villus (25 out of every 100 counted single-, double-, or triple-positive cells) than in the crypt (6 out of every 100 single-, double-, or triple-positive cells; Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The fraction of Cck+/Oc3+ cells decreased from 69.3% (±0.98%) in the crypt to 22.8% (±5.3%) in the villus.
source: Focusing on Oc3+ cells identified via smRNA-FISH, we found that the fraction of Cck+/Oc3+ cells decreased from 69.3% (±0.98%) in the crypt to 22.8% (±5.3%) in the villus, while Tph1+/Oc3+ cells increased from 17.3% (±2.4%) in the crypt to 38.0% (±3.2%) in the villus (Figure 3d), suggesting a likelihood that Cck+/Oc3+ double-positive cells gradually acquire the ability to generate Tph1 transcripts during their migration to the villus.
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Tph1+/Oc3+ cells increased from 17.3% (±2.4%) in the crypt to 38.0% (±3.2%) in the villus.
source: Focusing on Oc3+ cells identified via smRNA-FISH, we found that the fraction of Cck+/Oc3+ cells decreased from 69.3% (±0.98%) in the crypt to 22.8% (±5.3%) in the villus, while Tph1+/Oc3+ cells increased from 17.3% (±2.4%) in the crypt to 38.0% (±3.2%) in the villus (Figure 3d), suggesting a likelihood that Cck+/Oc3+ double-positive cells gradually acquire the ability to generate Tph1 transcripts during their migration to the villus.
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Cck+/Oc3+ double-positive cells gradually acquire the ability to generate Tph1 transcripts during their migration to the villus.
source: Focusing on Oc3+ cells identified via smRNA-FISH, we found that the fraction of Cck+/Oc3+ cells decreased from 69.3% (±0.98%) in the crypt to 22.8% (±5.3%) in the villus, while Tph1+/Oc3+ cells increased from 17.3% (±2.4%) in the crypt to 38.0% (±3.2%) in the villus (Figure 3d), suggesting a likelihood that Cck+/Oc3+ double-positive cells gradually acquire the ability to generate Tph1 transcripts during their migration to the villus.
evidence: Inferred from the differential distribution of Cck+/Oc3+ and Tph1+/Oc3+ cells along the crypt-villus axis.

claim: Crp was discretely expressed in cluster 6 by scRNA-seq and mapped to Cck+/Tph1+ cells by smRNA-FISH.
source: Specifically, discrete expression of Crp (encoding C-reactive protein) was identified in cluster 6 by scRNA-seq and mapped to Cck+/Tph1+ cells by smRNA-FISH (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Tlr2 was found in cluster 6 cells and validated by smRNA-FISH to be specific in Cck+/Tph1+ cells.
source: Similarly, several genes encoding molecules recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns were found in cluster 6 cells, including Tril (encoding TLR4 interactor with leucine rich repeats), Tlr2 (encoding Toll-like receptor 2) and Tlr5 (encoding Toll-like receptor 5). We validated the latter two by smRNA-FISH to be specific in Cck+/Tph1+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the notion that these cells play a role in pathogen or toxin recognition.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tlr5 was found in cluster 6 cells and validated by smRNA-FISH to be specific in Cck+/Tph1+ cells.
source: Similarly, several genes encoding molecules recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns were found in cluster 6 cells, including Tril (encoding TLR4 interactor with leucine rich repeats), Tlr2 (encoding Toll-like receptor 2) and Tlr5 (encoding Toll-like receptor 5). We validated the latter two by smRNA-FISH to be specific in Cck+/Tph1+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the notion that these cells play a role in pathogen or toxin recognition.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mc4r and Casr were distinctly identified in cluster 6 cells.
source: In addition to the unique signature of pathogen/toxin recognition, genes encoding G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) associated with nutrient sensing and energy homeostasis, Mc4r and Casr, were distinctly identified in cluster 6 cells (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Mc4r was validated by smRNA-FISH to be specific to Cck+/Tph1+ cells but not single-Tph1+ or -Cck+ cells.
source: We further validated expression of Mc4r and Casr by smRNA-FISH to be specific to Cck+/Tph1+ cells but not single-Tph1+ or -Cck+ cells (Figure 3h, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Casr was validated by smRNA-FISH to be specific to Cck+/Tph1+ cells but not single-Tph1+ or -Cck+ cells.
source: We further validated expression of Mc4r and Casr by smRNA-FISH to be specific to Cck+/Tph1+ cells but not single-Tph1+ or -Cck+ cells (Figure 3h, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among the Mc4r+ or Casr+ cells, >85% of them co-expressed at least one of the genes associated with pathogen/toxin recognition.
source: Although the nutrient sensing GPCRs were observed at relatively lower levels and frequencies in scRNA-seq data (Figure 3e, j), among the Mc4r+ or Casr+ cells, >85% of them co-expressed at least one of the genes associated with pathogen/toxin recognition (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A dual molecular signature associated with disparate functions can be resolved in the Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that a dual molecular signature associated with disparate functions can be resolved in the Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells.
evidence: Inferred from the co-expression of pathogen/toxin recognition genes and nutrient sensing genes in Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells.

claim: A discrete cluster with high levels of Cck, Sct, Tph1, and Ghrl, together with Gcg and Nts transcripts, was identified in the Neurod1+ EEC cells and annotated as a Cck+/Tph1+ cluster.
source: Among the Neurod1+ EEC cells, a discrete cluster with high levels of Cck, Sct, Tph1, and Ghrl, together with Gcg and Nts transcripts, was identified and annotated as a Cck+/Tph1+ cluster (Figure 3i, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3i and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oc3 and key signature genes resolved in cluster 6 were also specifically identified in the Cck+/Tph1+ population from the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset.
source: Oc3 and key signature genes resolved in cluster 6 were also specifically identified in this Cck+/Tph1+ population (Figure 3j, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3j and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Cck+/Tph1+ population in the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset is the equivalent of the cluster 6 in the Tph1-GFP dataset.
source: We thus conclude that the Cck+/Tph1+ population in the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset is the equivalent of the cluster 6 in the Tph1-GFP dataset.
evidence: Inferred from the shared molecular signatures between the two datasets.

claim: SI EC cells were preferentially enriched with Trpa1 and Trpm2 along with Cartpt and Ucn3 transcripts.
source: In support of our previous findings, SI EC cells were preferentially enriched with Trpa1 and Trpm2 along with Cartpt and Ucn3 transcripts.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Casr was enriched in the Cck+/Tph1+ cells.
source: Casr was enriched in the Cck+/Tph1+ cells, whereas Mc4r was primarily found in the Cck+/Tph1+ cells from the SI and additionally detected in distal colonic L cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Mc4r was primarily found in the Cck+/Tph1+ cells from the SI and additionally detected in distal colonic L cells.
source: Casr was enriched in the Cck+/Tph1+ cells, whereas Mc4r was primarily found in the Cck+/Tph1+ cells from the SI and additionally detected in distal colonic L cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset shown in Figure 3j.

claim: ~99% of Casr+ or Mc4r+ cells in the Cck+/Tph1+ cluster co-expressed at least one sensor gene associated with pathogen/toxin recognition.
source: Consistently with the findings from the Tph1-bacTRAP dataset, ~99% of Casr +or Mc4r+ cells in the Cck+/Tph1+ cluster co-expressed at least one sensor gene associated with pathogen/toxin recognition (Crp/Tlr2/Tlr5/Tril) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1j), in support of our observation that Cck+/Tph1+ cells are enriched with a dual sensory signature.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1j.

claim: Cnr1 was found and validated by smRNA-FISH to be enriched in the Gip-dominant K cell.
source: In the SI, Cnr1 (encoding CB1), Asic5 (encoding a bile acid sensitive ion channel (Basic)) (Wiemuth et al., 2014; Wiemuth et al., 2013), and Gper1 (encoding G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1, Gpr30) were found and validated by smRNA-FISH to be enriched in the Gip-dominant K cell (Moss et al., 2012), delta cells (Beumer et al., 2018), and K cells, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d, and citations to prior literature (Moss et al., 2012).

claim: Asic5 was found and validated by smRNA-FISH to be enriched in delta cells.
source: In the SI, Cnr1 (encoding CB1), Asic5 (encoding a bile acid sensitive ion channel (Basic)) (Wiemuth et al., 2014; Wiemuth et al., 2013), and Gper1 (encoding G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1, Gpr30) were found and validated by smRNA-FISH to be enriched in the Gip-dominant K cell (Moss et al., 2012), delta cells (Beumer et al., 2018), and K cells, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d, and citations to prior literature (Beumer et al., 2018).

claim: Gper1 was found and validated by smRNA-FISH to be enriched in K cells.
source: In the SI, Cnr1 (encoding CB1), Asic5 (encoding a bile acid sensitive ion channel (Basic)) (Wiemuth et al., 2014; Wiemuth et al., 2013), and Gper1 (encoding G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1, Gpr30) were found and validated by smRNA-FISH to be enriched in the Gip-dominant K cell (Moss et al., 2012), delta cells (Beumer et al., 2018), and K cells, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d.

claim: Stra6 was exclusively identified in distal colonic L cells and mapped to Pyy+ cells by smRNA-FISH.
source: In the colon, Stra6 (encoding a retinol transporter) was exclusively identified in distal colonic L cells and mapped to Pyy+ cells by smRNA-FISH (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e, f).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2e, f.

claim: Gpbar1 was found in the proximal/distal colonic L cells, rather than in the EC cells.
source: Gpbar1 (encoding a bile acid sensor Tgr5) was found in the proximal/distal colonic L cells, rather than in the EC cells. We further validated this finding by smRNA-FISH (Figure 3—figure supplement 2g, h) and by a similar finding from human mucosa single cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–k).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2g, h, and human data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–k.

claim: Ffar1 was found in almost all Cck+ cells, as well as in Gcg+ L cells from both SI and colon.
source: In contrast to these cluster-specific sensors, the long chain fatty acid receptor Ffar1 (Gpr40) was found in almost all Cck+ cells, as well as in Gcg+ L cells from both SI and colon.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Ffar2 was widely observed in all EEC cells except K cells.
source: Ffar2 (Gpr43) and Ffar3 (Gpr41/42) encode GPCRs that recognize microbial metabolites, the former of which we widely observed in all EEC cells except K cells, whereas the latter we primarily detected in the closely related L, I, and N cells (Figure 3j).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Ffar3 was primarily detected in the closely related L, I, and N cells.
source: Ffar2 (Gpr43) and Ffar3 (Gpr41/42) encode GPCRs that recognize microbial metabolites, the former of which we widely observed in all EEC cells except K cells, whereas the latter we primarily detected in the closely related L, I, and N cells (Figure 3j).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Almost all of the molecular sensors were confined to EEC cells, with little or no expression observed in other epithelial cell types.
source: Lastly, almost all of these molecular sensors were confined to EEC cells, with little or no expression observed in other epithelial cell types (Haber et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to prior literature (Haber et al., 2017).

claim: EC cells in the proximal colon encompassed two clusters: Iapp+/Cpb2+/Serpine1+/Sct+ cluster 11 and Il12a+/Olfr558+/Olfr78+/Tac1+ cluster 12.
source: In the proximal colon, EC cells encompassed two clusters: Iapp+/Cpb2+/Serpine1+/Sct+ cluster 11 and Il12a+/Olfr558+/Olfr78+/Tac1+ cluster 12 (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Proximal colonic EC cells were involved in coagulation regulation.
source: GO analysis indicated that proximal colonic EC cells were involved in coagulation regulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), which is supported by the selective expression of Cpb2 and Serpine1 (Figure 4a), encoding the two known plasmin inhibitors, thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI) and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), respectively.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and expression data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Iapp was validated in a subset of proximal colonic EC cells (cluster 11) by smRNA-FISH, but not in distal colonic EC cells.
source: Iapp was also validated in a subset of proximal colonic EC cells (cluster 11) by smRNA-FISH, but not in distal colonic EC cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Olfr558 and Olfr78 were enriched in cluster 12.
source: Olfr558 (encoding olfactory receptor 558) and Olfr78 (encoding olfactory receptor 78), two genes encoding GPCRs sensing short-chain fatty acids (Fleischer et al., 2015; Lund et al., 2018), were enriched in cluster 12 (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a, b and citations to prior literature (Fleischer et al., 2015; Lund et al., 2018).

claim: Il12a was concomitantly expressed in cluster 12 and validated by smRNA-FISH.
source: Il12a (Billing et al., 2019) (encoding interleukin-12 subunit alpha) was concomitantly expressed in this cluster (Figure 4a) and validated by smRNA-FISH (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4c, and citation to prior literature (Billing et al., 2019).

claim: Olfr558 and Il12a transcripts were mapped to a separate subset of EC cells expressing Cpb2 by smRNA-FISH.
source: Using smRNA-FISH, we further mapped Olfr558 and Il12a transcripts to a separate subset of EC cells expressing Cpb2 (Figure 4b, c), supporting the idea that there are subpopulations of EC cells in the proximal colon with gene transcripts associated with different physiological roles.
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: Ascl1 was found in the distal colonic EC cells (clusters 13 and 14).
source: Ascl1, encoding Mash1 (mammalian achaete-scute homolog 1), is required for early neural tube specification (Johnson et al., 1990; Lo et al., 1991; Pang et al., 2011; Wapinski et al., 2013). Unexpectedly, Ascl1 was found in the distal colonic EC cells (Figures 1e and 4a; clusters 13 and 14) and was exclusively mapped to Tph1+ cells but not to Pyy+ cells in the distal colon, nor to any cell of the proximal colon or jejunum in smRNA-FISH analysis (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 1e and 4a, and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, and citations to prior literature (Johnson et al., 1990; Lo et al., 1991; Pang et al., 2011; Wapinski et al., 2013).

claim: Ascl1 was exclusively mapped to Tph1+ cells but not to Pyy+ cells in the distal colon.
source: Ascl1, encoding Mash1 (mammalian achaete-scute homolog 1), is required for early neural tube specification (Johnson et al., 1990; Lo et al., 1991; Pang et al., 2011; Wapinski et al., 2013). Unexpectedly, Ascl1 was found in the distal colonic EC cells (Figures 1e and 4a; clusters 13 and 14) and was exclusively mapped to Tph1+ cells but not to Pyy+ cells in the distal colon, nor to any cell of the proximal colon or jejunum in smRNA-FISH analysis (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: ASCL1 was only detected in the TPH1+ cells from the rectum in human gut mucosa.
source: Importantly, this feature was conserved in the human gut mucosa, where ASCL1 was only detected in the TPH1+ cells from the rectum (HOXB13 high) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by human scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EC cells from the distal colon were overwhelmingly associated with GO terms 'neuron projection morphogenesis', 'axon development', and 'microtubule-based process'.
source: Prominently, EC cells from the distal colon, in contrast to their counterparts from other GI regions, were overwhelmingly associated with GO terms 'neuron projection morphogenesis', 'axon development', and 'microtubule-based process' (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Numerous genes indicative of neuronal identity were mutually enriched in distal colonic ECs.
source: Numerous genes indicative of neuronal identity were mutually enriched in distal colonic ECs (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: EC cells in the distal colon exhibited unique long basal processes, often extending for 50–100 µm, with 5-HT concentrated in the long processes.
source: Consistently, EC cells in the distal colon exhibited unique long basal processes, often extending for 50–100 µm, with 5-HT concentrated in the long processes, in contrast to the typical open-type, flask-shaped EEC cells observed in the proximal colon or SI (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1f; Koo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f, and citation to prior literature (Koo et al., 2021).

claim: Foxj1 and Dnah9 were selectively enriched in cluster 13.
source: In cluster 13, Foxj1 and Dnah9, encoding a TF (forkhead box protein J1) and an axonemal dynein (dynein heavy chain 9, axonemal) required for cilia formation (Lim et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2008), respectively, were selectively enriched (Figure 4a) and validated by smRNA-FISH in the distal colonic EC cells but not in the proximal colonic EC cells or Pyy+ L cells (Figure 4h, Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4h and Figure 4—figure supplement 1g, and citations to prior literature (Lim et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2008).

claim: Genes associated with GO terms 'cilium assembly/organization' were enriched in the distal colonic EC cells.
source: Genes associated with GO terms 'cilium assembly/organization' were also enriched in the distal colonic EC cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, h).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, h.

claim: Cilia were identified by immunostaining against intraflagellar transport protein 88 (IFT88) and found to exclusively co-stain with 5-HT.
source: Consistent with the molecule features, we identified cilia by immunostaining against intraflagellar transport protein 88 (IFT88), an essential component for axonemal transportation, and found exclusive co-staining of IFT88 with 5-HT (Figure 4i).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Piezo2 was identified in almost all EC cells in the distal colon.
source: Most prominently, in the distal colon, Piezo2, encoding a mechanosensitive ion channel, was identified in almost all EC cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: smRNA-FISH revealed robust expression of Piezo2 in the Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells residing in the epithelial layer of distal colon mucosa.
source: smRNA-FISH further revealed robust expression of Piezo2 in the Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells residing in the epithelial layer of distal colon mucosa (Figure 5a, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Low levels (1–5 puncta per cell) of Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria beneath the epithelium throughout the gut.
source: In addition, we noticed low levels (1–5 puncta per cell) of Piezo2 signals in the lamina propria beneath the epithelium throughout the gut which contains mainly immune cells and connective tissue cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Piezo1 transcripts were either undetectable or sparsely observed (1 or 2 puncta per cell) in epithelium and lamina propria.
source: In contrast to Piezo2, Piezo1 transcripts were either undetectable or sparsely observed (1 or 2 puncta per cell) in epithelium and lamina propria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Piezo2 was not detected in the Tph1+ cells from the proximal colon, ileum, jejunum, and duodenum via smRNA-FISH.
source: Piezo2 was not detected in the Tph1+ cells from the proximal colon, ileum, jejunum, and duodenum via smRNA-FISH (Figure 5b, c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5b, c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A significant enrichment of Piezo2, up to 360-fold, was observed in the GFP+ cells sorted from the distal colon, when compared to the GFP+ cells from duodenum, jejunum, or proximal colon or to the GFP− cells from the same regions.
source: To further evaluate the variation of Piezo2 expression, we sorted GFP− and GFP+ cells from various segments of the gut isolated in the Tph1-bacTRAP animals and quantitated Piezo2 and other newly identified signature genes by qPCR analysis (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and d). A significant enrichment of Piezo2, up to 360-fold, was observed in the GFP+ cells sorted from the distal colon, when compared to the GFP+ cells from duodenum, jejunum, or proximal colon or to the GFP− cells from the same regions.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Piezo2 is preferentially enriched in neuron-like distal colonic EC cells.
source: Based on multiple lines of evidence, we conclude that Piezo2 is preferentially enriched in neuron-like distal colonic EC cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined evidence of scRNA-seq, smRNA-FISH, and qPCR data.

claim: A concomitant expression of Piezo2 with Foxj1 and Olfr78 was revealed by scRNA-seq and validated by smRNA-FISH.
source: Furthermore, a concomitant expression of Piezo2 with Foxj1 and Olfr78 was revealed by scRNA-seq (Figure 4a, cluster 13) and validated by smRNA-FISH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i), which suggests that a subpopulation of Piezo2+/Tph1+ cells are mechanosensory cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i.

claim: A subpopulation of Piezo2+/Tph1+ cells are mechanosensory cells.
source: Furthermore, a concomitant expression of Piezo2 with Foxj1 and Olfr78 was revealed by scRNA-seq (Figure 4a, cluster 13) and validated by smRNA-FISH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i), which suggests that a subpopulation of Piezo2+/Tph1+ cells are mechanosensory cells.
evidence: Inferred from the co-expression of Piezo2, Foxj1, and Olfr78.

claim: 15 min after intracolonic administration of CNO, a robust elevation (2.1 ± 0.2 fold) of serum serotonin was observed in Piezo2-CHRM3* mice.
source: Fifteen minutes after intracolonic administration of CNO, a robust elevation (2.1 ± 0.2 fold) of serum serotonin was observed in Piezo2-CHRM3* mice, but not in WT, or Rosa26-LSL-CHRM3* mice following the same treatment, and no effect was observed with saline administration or in untreated animals (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: No elevation of serum serotonin was observed in WT or Rosa26-LSL-CHRM3* mice following CNO treatment.
source: Fifteen minutes after intracolonic administration of CNO, a robust elevation (2.1 ± 0.2 fold) of serum serotonin was observed in Piezo2-CHRM3* mice, but not in WT, or Rosa26-LSL-CHRM3* mice following the same treatment, and no effect was observed with saline administration or in untreated animals (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: In response to CNO stimulation, serotonin release from the mCitrine+/Epcam+ cells of distal colon was elevated by 1.9 (±0.19) fold.
source: Moreover, in response to CNO stimulation, serotonin release from the mCitrine+/Epcam+ cells of distal colon was elevated by 1.9 (±0.19) fold, whereas mCitrine−/Epcam+ cells failed to respond (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d e).
evidence: Supported by in vitro serotonin release assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d, e.

claim: mCitrine−/Epcam+ cells failed to respond to CNO stimulation.
source: Moreover, in response to CNO stimulation, serotonin release from the mCitrine+/Epcam+ cells of distal colon was elevated by 1.9 (±0.19) fold, whereas mCitrine−/Epcam+ cells failed to respond (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d e).
evidence: Supported by in vitro serotonin release assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d, e.

claim: CNO-mediated activation of Piezo2+ cells leads to robust serotonin release from epithelial EC cells.
source: Together, this data demonstrates that CNO-mediated activation of Piezo2+ cells leads to robust serotonin release from epithelial EC cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined evidence of serum serotonin elevation and in vitro serotonin release assays.

claim: Increased fecal pellet output was observed from the Piezo2-CHRM3* mice within 15 min after CNO administration.
source: We observed increased fecal pellet output from the Piezo2-CHRM3* mice within 15 min after CNO administration, in contrast to the WT controls (Figure 5g).
evidence: Supported by fecal pellet assay data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: In a bead expulsion assay, colon motility was significantly accelerated in Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals after CNO treatment, with the time to expel an inserted bead shortened from 7.24 (±2.0) min in wild-type controls to 1.16 (±1.17) min.
source: In a bead expulsion assay (BEA), colon motility was found to be significantly accelerated, such that the time to expel an inserted bead was shortened from 7.24 (±2.0) min in wild-type controls to 1.16 (±1.17) min in the Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals after CNO treatment, while no difference was observed between wild-type controls and Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals in untreated or saline treated cohorts (Figure 5h, Figure 5—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: Supported by bead expulsion assay data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: No difference in bead expulsion time was observed between wild-type controls and Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals in untreated or saline treated cohorts.
source: In a bead expulsion assay (BEA), colon motility was found to be significantly accelerated, such that the time to expel an inserted bead was shortened from 7.24 (±2.0) min in wild-type controls to 1.16 (±1.17) min in the Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals after CNO treatment, while no difference was observed between wild-type controls and Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals in untreated or saline treated cohorts (Figure 5h, Figure 5—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: Supported by bead expulsion assay data shown in Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 2f.

claim: Htr4 was selectively expressed by epithelium in the deep crypts of distal colon.
source: We noticed that Htr4, encoding the 5-HT4 receptor, a prokinetic 5-HT receptor when activated, was selectively expressed by epithelium in the deep crypts of distal colon (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The long basal processes of EC cells filled with 5-HT always extend toward the base of the crypts, where the Htr4 is preferentially expressed.
source: Meanwhile, the long basal processes of EC cells filled with 5-HT always extend toward the base of the crypts, where the Htr4 is preferentially expressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Profound co-depletion of Piezo2 and Tph1 transcripts was demonstrated by smRNA-FISH in the distal colon of the Piezo2-DTR mice after DT treatment.
source: Profound co-depletion of Piezo2 and Tph1 transcripts was demonstrated by smRNA-FISH in the distal colon of the Piezo2-DTR mice, but not in the proximal colon or in the WT mice receiving the same DT treatment (Figure 6b, c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 6b, c, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substantial loss of 5-HT+ cells was validated by immunofluorescence staining in the distal colon of Piezo2-DTR mice after DT treatment.
source: Substantial loss of 5-HT+ cells was further validated by immunofluorescence staining in the distal colon, but not in the proximal colon, while the general epithelial architecture was well maintained (Figure 6b, d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6b, d, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The general epithelial architecture was well maintained in Piezo2-DTR mice after DT treatment.
source: Substantial loss of 5-HT+ cells was further validated by immunofluorescence staining in the distal colon, but not in the proximal colon, while the general epithelial architecture was well maintained (Figure 6b, d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6b, d, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a 2-hr FPA, a 42% reduction in fecal pellet output was observed in the Piezo2-depleted mice compared to WT animals with the same treatment regimen.
source: In a 2-hr FPA, a 42% reduction in fecal pellet output was observed in the Piezo2-depleted mice compared to WT animals with the same treatment regimen (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by fecal pellet assay data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: BEA demonstrated a substantial delay (36.9 ± 19.1 min) to expel an inserted bead in the Piezo2-depleted mice compared to the WT controls (8.2 ± 1.9 min).
source: BEA demonstrated a substantial delay (36.9 ± 19.1 min) to expel an inserted bead in the Piezo2-depleted mice compared to the WT controls (8.2 ± 1.9 min) (Figure 6f), which was not observed in the Rosa26-LSL- DTR animals under the same treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by bead expulsion assay data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Gastric emptying was not affected in the Piezo2-DTR animals after DT treatment.
source: Although gastric emptying was not affected in the Piezo2-DTR animals after DT treatment, small intestine transit (SIT) time, a measurement to assess the motility of small intestine, presented a small but statistically significant slowdown in the former group (Figure 6g and h).
evidence: Supported by gastric emptying assay data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Small intestine transit (SIT) time presented a small but statistically significant slowdown in the Piezo2-DTR animals after DT treatment.
source: Although gastric emptying was not affected in the Piezo2-DTR animals after DT treatment, small intestine transit (SIT) time, a measurement to assess the motility of small intestine, presented a small but statistically significant slowdown in the former group (Figure 6g and h).
evidence: Supported by small intestine transit assay data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: The whole gut transit time was delayed in the Piezo2-DTR animals (181.8 ± 17.6 min) in comparison to WT (136.7 ± 9.3 min) under the same DT treatment.
source: Consistent with the retarded colon motility, the whole gut transit time was found to be delayed in the Piezo2-DTR animals (181.8 ± 17.6 min) in comparison to WT (136.7 ± 9.3 min, Figure 6i) under the same DT treatment.
evidence: Supported by whole gut transit time assay data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: 15.9% of the Villin-cre;Piezo2fl/fl mice (Piezo2 CKO) died around 21–34 days after birth.
source: Unexpectedly, 15.9% of the Villin-cre;Piezo2fl/fl mice (referred to as Piezo2 CKO hereafter) died around 21–34 days after birth, affecting both males and females.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: By the time of humane euthanasia, the affected Piezo2 CKO animals presented a 42% reduction of body weight and runt body size.
source: By the time of humane euthanasia, the affected animals presented a 42% reduction of body weight and runt body size (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–c, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by body weight data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: Piezo2 depletion was observed from the isolated epithelial layer of the distal colon in Piezo2 CKO mice, as assessed by qPCR.
source: Piezo2 depletion was observed from the isolated epithelial layer of the distal colon, as assessed by qPCR (Figure 7a, Figure 7—source data 1) and smRNA-FISH analysis (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7a and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Tph1 and Chga levels remained unaltered in the Piezo2 CKO animals assessed by qPCR.
source: Meanwhile, Tph1 and Chga levels remained unaltered in the Piezo2 CKO animals assessed by qPCR (Figure 7c, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7c and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No change was observed in basal serotonin levels from either the epithelial tissue or the serum in Piezo2 CKO animals.
source: Consistently, no change was observed in basal serotonin levels from either the epithelial tissue or the serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1g, h).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1g, h.

claim: Residual signals of Piezo2 were observed in some of the Tph1+ cells of the distal colon in the Piezo2 CKO animals.
source: Notably, residual signals of Piezo2 were observed in some of the Tph1+ cells of the distal colon in the Piezo2 CKO animals (Figure 7b), suggesting incomplete depletion.
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Piezo2 signals in the lamina propria remained largely unaltered in Piezo2 CKO animals.
source: Importantly, Piezo2 signals in the lamina propria remained largely unaltered (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1i, j), suggesting that only the epithelial Piezo2 was abolished in this mouse line.
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1i, j.

claim: A significant slowing of expulsion was revealed by BEA in the Piezo2 CKO mice (male 33.7 ± 19.0 min, female 32.3 ± 18.1 min) compared with littermate Piezo2fl/fl controls (male 9.25 ± 2.2 min, female 8.9 ± 1.5 min).
source: Lastly, we measured BEA and total GI transit time. A significant slowing of expulsion was revealed by BEA in the Piezo2 CKO mice (male 33.7 ± 19.0 min, female 32.3 ± 18.1 min) compared with littermate Piezo2fl/fl controls (male 9.25 ± 2.2 min, female 8.9 ± 1.5 min, Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by bead expulsion assay data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Prolonged whole gut transit time was observed in Piezo2 CKO mice (male 182 ± 17.5 min, female 175 ± 15.6 min) compared to littermate Piezo2fl/fl controls (male 146 ± 11.7 min, female 143 ± 13.7 min).
source: In addition, prolonged whole gut transit time was observed in Piezo2 CKO mice (male 182 ± 17.5 min, female 175 ± 15.6 min) compared to littermate Piezo2fl/fl controls (male 146 ± 11.7 min, female 143 ± 13.7 min; Figure 7e).
evidence: Supported by whole gut transit time assay data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: No difference was observed in SIT between Piezo2 CKO mice (95.9 ± 2.6%) versus Piezo2fl/fl controls (96.6 ± 2.2%).
source: To assess small intestinal transit, mice were euthanized 70 min after gavage of a fluorescent dye and the travel distance of the dye within the intestine was calculated as a percentage of total small intestinal length. No difference was observed in SIT between Piezo2 CKO mice (95.9 ± 2.6%) versus Piezo2fl/fl controls (96.6 ± 2.2%, Figure 7—figure supplement 1k), in contrast to the DTR experiments, in which small intestinal transit was delayed.
evidence: Supported by small intestinal transit assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1k.

claim: Fluorescent dye travel distance as a percentage of total colon length at 120 min after oral gavage was significantly shorter (51.2 ± 5.6%) in the Piezo2 CKO mice compared to Piezo2fl/fl controls (72.1 ± 4.1%).
source: We then assessed fluorescent dye travel distance as a percentage of total colon length at 120 min after oral gavage, which was significantly shorter (51.2 ± 5.6%) in the Piezo2 CKO mice compared to Piezo2fl/fl controls (72.1 ± 4.1%, Figure 7f, g).
evidence: Supported by colon transit assay data shown in Figure 7f, g.

claim: Loss of Piezo2 in epithelial EC cells primarily affected colon motility.
source: Taken together, loss of Piezo2 in epithelial EC cells primarily affected colon motility.
evidence: Inferred from the combined evidence of bead expulsion assay, whole gut transit time, and colon transit assays.

claim: Piezo2+/Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells are required for normal colon motility.
source: Collectively, our in vivo gain- and loss-of-function analyses demonstrated that Piezo2+/Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells are required for normal colon motility.
evidence: Inferred from the combined evidence of chemogenetic activation and genetic depletion experiments.

claim: 14 EC subpopulations were resolved characterized by their expression of distinct chemical and mechanical sensors, TFs, subcellular structures, and explicit spatial distribution within the gut mucosa.
source: In this study, we integrated high-throughput single-cell RNA-sequencing with spatial imaging analysis and constructed an ontological and topographical map for EC cells in mouse intestine (Figure 8). We resolved 14 EC subpopulations characterized by their expression of distinct chemical and mechanical sensors, TFs, subcellular structures, and explicit spatial distribution within the gut mucosa (Figure 7h).
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive scRNA-seq and spatial imaging data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The transcriptome diversity of EC cells is closely related to their spatial distribution.
source: We demonstrate that the transcriptome diversity of EC cells is closely related to their spatial distribution.
evidence: Inferred from the regional and crypt-villus axis-specific expression patterns observed in the scRNA-seq data.

claim: The first layer of complexity in EC cells is defined along the rostro-caudal axis, between the small intestine and the colon.
source: The first layer of complexity is defined along the rostro-caudal axis, between the small intestine and the colon (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by the regional clustering and differential expression analysis shown throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: A gradual enrichment of a neuron-like transcriptome is observed from small intestine to proximal and distal colon.
source: Together with a host of TFs defining the rostro-caudal axis, we observe a gradual enrichment of a neuron-like transcriptome from small intestine to proximal and distal colon, such that Ascl1, encoding a key TF required for early neural fate commitment (Johnson et al., 1990; Lo et al., 1991), is specifically expressed in the distal colonic EC cells.
evidence: Supported by the expression data and GO analysis shown in Figures 1e, 4a, 4e, and citations to prior literature (Johnson et al., 1990; Lo et al., 1991).

claim: A second layer of complexity in EC cells is resolved along the crypt–villus axis.
source: We resolved a second layer of complexity along the crypt–villus axis for the EC cells in a similar manner as described in EEC cells and enterocytes (Billing et al., 2019; Moor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by the differential expression analysis along the crypt-villus axis shown in Figure 2a and citations to prior literature (Billing et al., 2019; Moor et al., 2018).

claim: Piezo2 is preferentially expressed in distal colonic EC cells that also have neuronal expression profiles.
source: By combining scRNA-seq profiling from two different genetic models, smRNA-FISH and in vivo genetic ablation, our study demonstrated that Piezo2 is preferentially expressed in distal colonic EC cells that also have neuronal expression profiles.
evidence: Supported by the combined evidence from scRNA-seq, smRNA-FISH, and genetic ablation experiments shown in Figures 4a, 5a-d, 6b-i, and 7a-g.

claim: Depletion of Piezo2 from distal colonic EC cells caused a fourfold increase in bead expulsion time.
source: Depletion of Piezo2 from these cells caused a fourfold increase in bead expulsion time, implying that the mechanical stimulus provided by the bead caused 5-HT release and the initiation of colon propulsion.
evidence: Supported by bead expulsion assay data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: 5-HT released from EC has been shown to cause colorectal propulsion in mice.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, in other studies in mice, 5-HT released from EC has been shown to cause colorectal propulsion (Pustovit et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Pustovit et al., 2021).

claim: Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria throughout the intestine.
source: In addition, Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria throughout the intestine.
evidence: Supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Piezo2 was detected via scRNA-seq in a subset of sensory DRG neuron innervating the colon.
source: Given the previous report that Piezo2 was detected via scRNA-seq in a subset of sensory DRG neuron innervating the colon (Hockley et al., 2019), it is possible that both distal colonic EC cells and the sensory DRG neurons contribute to mechanosensory sensing and motility control.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Hockley et al., 2019).

claim: Both distal colonic EC cells and sensory DRG neurons may contribute to mechanosensory sensing and motility control.
source: Given the previous report that Piezo2 was detected via scRNA-seq in a subset of sensory DRG neuron innervating the colon (Hockley et al., 2019), it is possible that both distal colonic EC cells and the sensory DRG neurons contribute to mechanosensory sensing and motility control.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of Piezo2 in both EC cells and DRG neurons.

claim: A cluster of Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ EC cells identified in the duodenal villi was enriched with two sets of sensory molecules: enzymes/receptors associated with pathogen/toxin recognition and receptors associated with nutrient sensing and homeostasis.
source: A cluster of Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ EC cells identified in the duodenal villi was enriched with two sets of sensory molecules: enzymes/receptors associated with pathogen/toxin recognition (Crp, Lyzl4, Bcam, Tril, Tlr2, and Tlr5) and receptors associated with nutrient sensing and homeostasis (Casr and Mc4r), suggesting a that these cells react to gastric content entering the duodenum.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figures 3e-h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ cells may react to gastric content entering the duodenum.
source: A cluster of Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ EC cells identified in the duodenal villi was enriched with two sets of sensory molecules: enzymes/receptors associated with pathogen/toxin recognition (Crp, Lyzl4, Bcam, Tril, Tlr2, and Tlr5) and receptors associated with nutrient sensing and homeostasis (Casr and Mc4r), suggesting a that these cells react to gastric content entering the duodenum.
evidence: Inferred from the dual sensory signature of Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ cells.

claim: The gut has a well-established defensive role to expel noxious chemicals and toxins by nausea and vomiting that is initiated by 5-HT release and can be effectively inhibited by 5-HT3 receptor antagonists.
source: The gut has a well-established defensive role to expel noxious chemicals and toxins by nausea and vomiting that is initiated by 5-HT release and can be effectively inhibited by 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (Mawe and Hoffman, 2013; Andrews et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Mawe and Hoffman, 2013; Andrews et al., 1998).

claim: Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ cells equipped with pathogen/toxin recognition receptors may play a role in the defense mechanism to expel noxious chemicals and toxins.
source: Our findings suggests that Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ cells equipped with pathogen/toxin recognition receptors may play a role in this defense mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of pathogen/toxin recognition receptors in Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ cells and the known role of 5-HT in gut defense.
